speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege.
On Monday, July 8, 1963, as recorded on page 1968 of Hansard, the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) made a commitment to some hon. members, and more particularly the member for Lapointe.
At that time I had asked the Secretary of State the following question on Bills C-83 and C-84: If the committee is ready to sit, and the Secretary of State can assure us that it will and sit before the bill is presented, then we will agree to the bill being read for the first time. The Secretary of State answered:
I would be quite prepared to give an undertaking that in some fashion or other this matter would be remitted to a committee so that the matters the hon. member wishes to raise could be raised, if that is satisfactory.
I wish to point out that it was to the member for Lapointe that the Secretary of State was speaking, when he said:
-so that the matters the hon. member wishes to raise could be raised.
The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) confirmed that promise, as can be seen on the same page of Hansard:
I would confirm the undertaking given by the house leader that we will have a committee set up suitable to the hon. member where these matters can be discussed.
Further on-and here the matter becomes clearcut-the Secretary of State said as recorded on the same page of Hansard:
Once these two bills are seen, if there is any demand from any quarter of the house that some of the matters in the bills or other matters related to them could usefully be reviewed by a committee, I will undertake to ask my colleagues to have this done, and I feel sure they would agree with me. In fact, I am quite prepared to commit the government to putting a motion on the order paper for a reference to a suitable standing committee of the house to consider these matters before we proceed with the legislation itself.
Mr. Speaker, I can give further proof of what I am saying by referring to Hansard of October 11, 1963, page 3469, left hand column. The Secretary of State said on that date:
Mr. Speaker, there is absolutely no question that I did make a very precise commitment and I intend to carry out that commitment if there is any insistence on the part of any hon. member that I do so. The commitment was to refer a specific matter-
Mr. Speaker, that specific matter was the frontiers of the Northwest Territories, as it will be seen in a moment.
I continue with my quotation:
The commitment was to refer a specific matter, namely the frontiers, to the consideration of the committee before we proceed with the bill.
Mr. Speaker, those were formal and definite commitments on the part of the Secretary of State and of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. And I think that at one time the Secretary of State mentioned that it was precisely the matter of northern frontiers that was referred to the committee on mines, forests and waters. Indeed, the Secretary of State stated, a little further:
But if the hon. member or any other hon. member wishes to insist that the matters raised in the debate, that is to say, the question of the frontiers of the territories, should be considered separately first by a committee, I will endeavour to consult with whoever raises objection, the hon. member for Lapointe or anyone else, and try to draft some kind of motion to refer the matter to some suitable committee and bring it forward for debate.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the committee was specifically set up to study that problem. Now, the chairman of the committee, the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Godin) and the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Turner), have violated the commitments-

subtopic: MR. GREGOIRE    COMMITTEE CONSIDERATION OF BILLS C-83 AND C-84
speechtext:
But in order to help the house and the hon. member I have given some thought to this question, which fortunately I anticipated might arise. May I say that the so-called question of privilege raised today is in effect an appeal to the house from the ruling of the chairman on a proceeding in a standing committee, and I must say I question very seriously the regularity of this procedure at this time.
The first precedent in this regard arose in 1956, when the chairman of the standing committee on banking and commerce reported that his ruling had been appealed in the committee and he submitted the question to the judgment of the house. This is recorded at page 6388 of Hansard of July 24, 1956. Mr. Speaker Beaudoin in part dealt with the question as follows:
I have to rule now that the appeal from the chairman's ruling should he settled in the committee on banking and commerce and not reported to this house.
This matter is referred to in Beauchesne, fourth edition, page 241, citation 295, which reads in part as follows:
On July 24, 1956, an appeal was taken to the house from the standing committee on banking and commerce, and the Speaker ruled that the chairman's ruling should be settled in the committee and not reported to the house.
The second precedent in this regard is found on Wednesday, August 6, 1958, page 3141 of Hansard. Following the first precedent Mr. Speaker Michener stated among other things:

it must be stated that there is no known precedent wherein the Speaker of the house has acted either as arbitrator or as judge in connection with the regularity of any proceedings in any committee of the house.-I find, therefore, that it would not be practicable for the Speaker, nor would it be competent for him, to review a ruling upon a regularity of a proceeding in a standing committee. This decision, of course, does not interfere with or deprive the house of its jurisdiction over its standing committees and their reports.
On the matter of the jurisdiction of the committee I could follow this up with the following quotation from May's Parliamentary Practice, sixteenth edition, page 655, under the heading, "Reporting of Bills to the House

Division
Before Their Consideration Has Been Concluded". I am giving this detail because I think it might be useful to all hon. members.
It is the duty of standing committees, as of all committees, to give the matters referred to them due and sufficient consideration. Accordingly, the chairman of a standing committee will not accept a motion that the committee do not proceed further with the consideration of a bill from a member who is not in charge of the bill, nor will he accept a motion for reporting a bill to the house before its consideration has been completed by the committee, or any other motion which conflicts with the obligations imposed on the committee by the house.
Bourinot's Parliamentary Procedure, fourth edition, page 520, also says:
Every committee on a public bill is bound to report thereon. The house alone has power to prevent its passage or to order its withdrawal.
Beauchesne, fourth edition, citation 506, says:
Every bill referred to the committee must be reported.
And later:
It is the duty of every committee to report to the house the bill that has been committed to them-*
In this connection I might refer hon. members to standing order 109.
On the subject of an order of reference, an indication by a minister of the crown that something may be done in the committee is not a part of the order of reference.
On June 19, 1924, Mr. Speaker Lemieux stated, as found in Hansard, page 3389:
Under the rules and customs of British parliaments, standing committees are not administrative bodies and their power is limited by such orders or instructions as may be given the house.
For the reasons I have given I am of the opinion that there is no question of privilege involved, nor is there any point of order which would justify my interference with the proceedings of the committee in question.

subtopic: * INVESTIGATION OF UNIDENTIFIED FLYING OBJECTS
* INVESTIGATION OF UNIDENTIFIED FLYING OBJECTS
speechtext:
1.	Is Canada co-operating with the special United States program for investigation of unidentified flying objects and, if so, is this entitled "Project Magnet"?
2.	Is "Project Magnet" an unpublicized worldwide operation, using specially equipped, super constellations, non-uniformed pilots and civilian scientists?
3.	Was the late Wilbert B. Smith, a government scientist, the head of the Canadian section of the U.F.O. research operation?
4.	Is any data available from "Project Magnet" to the general public?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: * INVESTIGATION OF UNIDENTIFIED FLYING OBJECTS
speechtext:
1. The R.C.A.F. co-operates with the United States in the investigation of reports of unidentified flying objects as in other matters of mutual interest, but not as part of a special program. The United States program known as "Project Magnet" is not directed to the investigation of unidentified flying objects.
2.	"Project Magnet" is a program conducted by the naval oceanographic office of the U.S. navy concerned with the compilation of geomagnetic data covering all the oceans of the world. The data are obtained in survey flights of U.S. navy aircraft carrying civilian scientists. Information concerning this program has been freely available for some years to interested scientists.
3.	Between December, 1950 and August, 1954 a small program of investigation in the field of geo-magnetics was carried out by the


then telecommunications division of the Department of Transport with a view to obtaining, if possible, some physical information or facts which might help to explain the phenomenon which was generally referred to as unidentified flying objects. Mr. W. B. Smith was the engineer in charge of this program.
4.	It is understood that data obtained in "Project Magnet", in the form of geo-magnetic charts, is available upon application to the naval oceanographic office of the U.S. navy.

C.B.C. EXPENDITURES FOR CANADIAN PERFORMERS
speechtext:
1.	Has the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation expanded, in the course of the current fiscal year, the proportion of its budget spent in Canada on Canadian performers?
2.	What proportion of its budget is spent for this purpose?
3.	Have any measures been taken by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, of the current year, to increase the Canadian content of programs and, if so, what are these measures?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: C.B.C. EXPENDITURES FOR CANADIAN PERFORMERS
speechtext:
I am informed by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as follows:
1.	The corporation does not assign on a proportionate basis a specified amount of its over-all program budget to be spent on Canadian performers. It prefers to allow greater flexibility to meet the variation in program needs and availabilities. Therefore it is not possible to give a categorical yes or no answer to the question. However, it can be said that, as the present winter program schedule gets underway, the indications are for an expansion in the over-all amount paid to Canadian performers.
2.	See No. 1.
3.	Measures have been taken by increasing the weekly amount of television network programming thereby opening up more opportunities for Canadian performers in C.B.C. produced programs, as well as those produced by other Canadian sources for the C.B.C. television network. It should be noted that the C.B.C. French and English networks carry a considerably higher percentage of Canadian content programs than the 55 per cent required by the B.B.G. For the year ending October 12, 1963, the English t.v. network carried 63 per cent Canadian, 6 per cent commonwealth, 31 per cent foreign and the French t.v. network carried 62 per cent Canadian, 15 per cent commonwealth, and 23 per cent foreign, programming.

FILM BOARD PRODUCTION "FIELDS OF SACRIFICE"
speechtext:
1.	What is the nature and character of the national film board production "Fields of Sacrifice" and, why was it produced?
2.	Who were the persons principally responsible for its production and, what were their qualifications?

3.	What actual battle scenes are shown and, what areas are revisited in modern technicolour?
4.	How can the Canadian public see this film and, when, and how will it be available for distribution to interested groups?
Answer: 1. The national film board production "Fields of Sacrifice" or "Champs d'hon-neur" is made up of a 40 minute film in English and in French and a 20 minute version in English and in French. It is in colour except for flash-back sequences. It was made in two lengths in order to achieve the widest distribution.
This production was commissioned by the Department of Veterans Affairs to recall the courage and sacrifice of Canadian servicemen during the 1914-18 and 1939-45 wars and to show Canadians, particularly the next of kin of those who died, how the memory of Canada's war dead is honoured and cherished in the countries where they fell. It is also designed to give renewed and vital meaning to the spirit of remembrance to the comrades of the war dead, to their next of kin and to those who were too young to know them at all.
2.	Executive producer, Peter Jones; producer, director, writer, Donald Brittain; director of photography, Eugene Boyko; film editor, Rex Tasker; music composed by Eldon Rathburn; editor of sound effects, Victor Merrill; rerecording, Ron Alexander, Roger Lamoureux; French production, Marcel Martin, Edouard Davidovici; author of French text, Gilles Henault; narration, Douglas Rain, Christian Delmas.
3.	Battle scenes:	Normandy invasion,
Dieppe, Sicily, Ortona, Dutch canals, Ypres, various unidentifiable photographs of world war I action on the western front.
Areas revisited: Normandy beaches, Normandy villages inland including Beny-sur-Mer and Bayeux, Hong Kong, Dieppe, Londonderry, Boxstead airfield, Reichswald forest, Runnymede, Agira, Cassino, Ortona, Bergen-op-Zoom, Groesbeek, Ypres, Mons, Arras, Armentieres, Poperinghe, various cemeteries in western front area including Beaumont Hamel, Quesnel, Bourlon wood, Dury, Sanctuary wood, Passchendaele, Cour-celette, St. Julien, Vimy Ridge. Also German cemetery at Langemarck.
4.	"Fields of Sacrifice" and "Champs d'hon-neur" are being distributed theatrically through Columbia Pictures of Canada Limited, and are available to every theatre in Canada. Non-theatrical release will commence July 1, 1964. The films will then be available to any individual or group across Canada through national film board sources, film councils, public libraries, etc.

maintopic: EFFECT ON CANADIAN INDUSTRY OF U.S. TARIFF RECLASSIFICATION
speechtext:
The hon. member will probably recall from my statement in the house on November 12 that uncertainties created for all Canadian exporters as a result of the recent introduction of a complete revision of the United States tariff nomenclature were under discussion with the United States. These discussions are continuing. It will be recalled that the question relates to whether certain items shipped to the United States should be classified under the new United States tariff language as parts or as manufactures of the metals or other materials from which they are made. Auto parts are definitely involved and could if preliminary classifications are upheld, be subject in certain cases to rate increases such as the hon. member has mentioned.
However, the United States bureau of customs has not ruled on these classification questions. In the meantime we are in constant touch with the United States government and will of course insist that Canadian interests be safeguarded.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if I may answer the second part of the hon. member's question, the bottles or glass were found in shipments from different ports, both those under the jurisdiction of the national harbours board and those under other jurisdictions.

maintopic: FINDING OF GLASS IN SHIPMENTS TO RUSSIA
speechtext: Is there not available a report following the inquiries made into contamination of shipments made to Great Britain?

maintopic: FINDING OF GLASS IN SHIPMENTS TO RUSSIA
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, there is not.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the minister what quantity of grain was affected by this contamination?

maintopic: FINDING OF GLASS IN SHIPMENTS TO RUSSIA
speechtext: I cannot tell that, but I think the stories on the subject, if I may use the term as comprising a lack of precision, appear to have been magnified quite materially. maintopic: FINDING OF GLASS IN SHIPMENTS TO RUSSIA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister of Justice a question that is supplementary to the previous one. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: FINDING OF GLASS IN SHIPMENTS TO RUSSIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to answer that
Inquiries of the Ministry question. Neither the officials of the Department of Justice nor the R.C.M.P. have received any information to that effect. maintopic: FINDING OF GLASS IN SHIPMENTS TO RUSSIA
speechtext: Could the Minister of Transport or the Minister of Trade and Commerce tell us when the house will be given a report arising from these investigations, and also what steps are being taken in the meantime to prevent a recurrence of this unfortunate incident?

maintopic: FINDING OF GLASS IN SHIPMENTS TO RUSSIA
speechtext: Perhaps I could add to something I said on the former question. There is no suggestion in this that there is a conspiracy, sabotage, or irregular action of that sort. It appears to be a matter of pure carelessness of persons who are working in very dusty conditions, and I may say-

maintopic: FINDING OF GLASS IN SHIPMENTS TO RUSSIA
speechtext: They don't like water.

maintopic: FINDING OF GLASS IN SHIPMENTS TO RUSSIA
speechtext: Well, they like the contents of a little glass, and if anyone saw the kind of work they have to do that would be well understood. Now, Mr. Speaker, this occurrence should not be permitted to get out of perspective. It is a very serious matter, but there is no suggestion of sabotage or anything like that involved. As a matter of fact, since the F.L.Q. was mentioned, I have to report that some of the bottles were found in two railway cars that had come from Ontario shipping points, one of which was a carload of soybeans.

maintopic: FINDING OF GLASS IN SHIPMENTS TO RUSSIA
speechtext: I asked the minister whether a report would be made.

maintopic: FINDING OF GLASS IN SHIPMENTS TO RUSSIA
speechtext: Yes, I want to answer the question of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. As soon as I can get anything to report to the house I shall be glad to do so. In the meantime steps are being taken to deal with the problem.

maintopic: FINDING OF GLASS IN SHIPMENTS TO RUSSIA
speechtext: What are they?

maintopic: FINDING OF GLASS IN SHIPMENTS TO RUSSIA
speechtext:
Perhaps I could indicate some of them. Very close attention is being given this matter by the board of grain commissioners, the national harbours board, the other harbour authorities, the other grain shipping people and the shipping interests, because it would appear that the bottles are going in after the grain is on the ships. The kind of remedial measures taken can be illustrated by the fact that in one particular harbour the agency which sells soft drinks no longer uses bottles, but paper cups.

Inquiries of the Ministry

maintopic: FINDING OF GLASS IN SHIPMENTS TO RUSSIA

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to put a question to the Minister of Transport. speakeroldname: Hon. G. J. Mcllrailh (Minisier of Transpori):
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA AIR LINES REPORTED DISPUTE CONCERNING JURISDICTION OVER CRASH INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have seen some of these reports. There is no jurisdictional dispute whatever between the two authorities. I think perhaps, because of the seriousness of the matter, I should explain my answer a little further by saying there is concurrent federal and provincial responsibility and jurisdiction in regard to investigation of the T.C.A. aircraft accident which occurred last Friday.
Under the Quebec coroners act and the Quebec police act responsibility for investigating circumstances relating to deaths, and authority for such investigation, is established. Similarly, in the Aeronautics Act and the air regulations made thereunder federal responsibility and authority exists for investigation of the accident to the aircraft; and, as I announced on Monday, steps have already
Inquiries of the Ministry been taken to set up a very extensive investigation under federal authority and control. There are, in effect, two sources of authority for investigation, provincial and federal. The provincial authorities are acting in accordance with their area of responsibility, while the federal investigation is proceeding under federal authority and responsibility. Both are working in close collaboration and in a spirit of mutual co-operation and assistance in this regard.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. J. Mcllraiih (Minister of Transport) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CHARGES FOR USE OF FACILITIES AND SERVICES
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-117, to amend the Aeronautics Act.
He said: A bill containing a large part of what appears in the measure now before the house was given first reading by the last parliament but because of the dissolution of that parliament it was not proceeded with. Perhaps I should outline briefly the principles included in the existing bill.
At the outset let me explain that the amendments are primarily intended to clarify and strengthen existing legislation and to make provision for fees and charges, some of which are now collected pursuant to the Financial Administration Act. Fields with which the amendments deal are fields in which the department is already active. The department's efforts in these fields have been taken under the general over-all authority of the Financial Administration Act and part I of the Aeronautics Act, but the experience which we have had has led us to believe that on a number of points our authority and our responsibility should be more clearly spelled out. I will review these points briefly.
The bill provides for regulations prescribing charges in respect of aircraft and airports. At present, charges are levied under air services fees regulations made under the authority of the Financial Administration Act. This act provides in part that fees may be prescribed by regulation charging the whole or part of the cost of any service to the person or persons for whom it is provided. Some of the facilities required by modern aircraft in the air and at airports are not encompassed by the word "service", and accordingly it is considered desirable to broaden the base on which charges may be levied. To accomplish this purpose it is felt that it would be better to place the authority

for charges in respect of aircraft and airports in the Aeronautics Act. The amendment would permit the government to deal with the situation which developed recently when it was decided to withdraw the route facility fee which had been imposed in January, 1960, under the authority of the Financial Administration Act. There is serious doubt that the Financial Administration Act authorizes this charge.
The bill also provides for regulations respecting the maximum hours of work and other working conditions for pilots, co-pilots, navigators and flight engineers employed by any person operating a commercial air service licensed by the air transport board. The complexity of the larger aircraft of today, the speeds at which they travel and the ever-increasing number of aircraft now in operation require flight crews to be at a peak of physical and mental efficiency during flight. To ensure this standard of efficiency it is necessary that the crew members do not remain on duty for excessive periods of time and be not required to work under conditions which are detrimental to safety.
There is provision for regulations to be made respecting the entering of the premises of any aircraft manufacturer and the inspecting of those premises, including any equipment, stock or records found therein, for the purpose of determining the airworthiness of aircraft manufactured by that manufacturer. No aircraft manufactured in Canada may be put to civil use unless it is airworthy and fit and safe in all respects for flight. It is the department's responsibility to ensure this; and to do this it is necessary to obtain complete information on the aircraft, including its parts and components and the facilities and equipment available to its builder.
There is also provision for regulations respecting the preservation and removal of aircraft involved in accidents, including the cargo thereof, and the preservation, removal and testing of any part of the aircraft. All hon. members will be particularly sensitive in these recent days to the fact that it is of the utmost importance that the exact cause of an aircraft accident should be determined, since this knowledge may serve to avert other mishaps. If the cause of an accident is to be determined, however, then it may be necessary to retain custody of the aircraft and its cargo and to remove and test any part of the aircraft.
Provision is also made for regulations respecting the use and operation of rockets, moored balloons and kites that, in the opinion of the governor in council, are hazardous to air navigation. It is rather interesting to note here that in more recent times the firing of rockets for military and scientific purposes 28902-5-3464
Aeronautics Act
has engendered intense public interest in this field of endeavour, so much so that we now have the amateur rocketeer constructing and firing his own rockets. Many of these do-it-yourself rockets are capable of reaching considerable altitudes and, although it has not happened yet in Canada, aircraft in flight have already suffered damage from these missiles. Although they have been with us for a considerably longer period of time, the moored balloon and kite are also something of a hazard to aircraft in flight, particularly when flown in close proximity to an aerodrome.
Another provision would vest the Canadian courts with jurisdiction in respect of offences against air regulations committed outside Canada. The Aeronautics Act already authorizes the making of regulations respecting the conditions under which aircraft registered in Canada may be operated outside Canada, but it does not confer jurisdiction on any Canadian court in respect of such offences committed ex juris.
Finally, the bill would authorize the establishment of boards of inquiry to investigate aircraft accidents or any alleged violations of the regulations, and would give such boards the necessary powers to fulfil their tasks properly and provide for the payment of witnesses' expenses. This amendment is particularly important as regards aircraft accidents since, if the cause of the accident is to be determined, it may require the establishment of a board armed with sufficient authority to summon and examine witnesses under oath. Hitherto this right has not been given specifically under the act.
I consider the bill to be a forward step. I consider that it will improve the financial position of the department in the operation of airports and route facilities, and it will also advance the safety of air travel in Canada. I would hope the bill would commend itself to the house. As I indicated in my opening remarks, a very substantial part of it was brought forward by the previous government but was not proceeded with by reason of the dissolution of that parliament. Those parts are reincorporated in this bill, together with some new material, as I have indicated in my speech.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the minister for the explanation he has given of the bill now before us. It is a fact that such a bill was brought to the attention of the house in a previous session and from what I can gather from the minister's remarks only a few changes have been made in the bill.
I am interested in the indication in the minister's remarks that the department has

Aeronautics Act
decided to give up its regulation with regard to route facility fees. I know that in the past this has always been a sore point with the foreign carriers. The matter was brought before the courts and I do not think the position of Canada in this regard was too sound legally. subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CHARGES FOR USE OF FACILITIES AND SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have some pertinent remarks to make with respect to the general principles involved in the bill, as well as the individual clauses of the bill itself. I feel that one of the most serious threats to the efficient use of private aircraft is the present attitude of Canada's air transport board. I speak as one who is quite familiar with the air transport board's operations and the regulations made under the Aeronautics Act because I come in contact with them constantly. I fly my own aircraft and use the airports right across this country and in the United States. I feel that there are three real threats to the growth of private flying in Canada. One, as I have already stated, is the attitude of the air transport board, and the other two are related because as our commercial air industry grows the tendency is for the government, and rightly so in certain respects, through the air transport board to design their regulations and their laws to favour the commercial sector of the aircraft industry in Canada.
The air transport board, I think, readily admits that one of the purposes of its existence is to deter private flying to the extent that private flying may interfere with the efficient operation of commercial carriers. If private flying detracts from the revenues of commercial air lines, then there is an immediate tendency to protect the sources of revenue of the commercial carriers. There are specific sections in the bill, for instance, which impose fees on airplanes using the Department of Transport facilities. The commercial air carriers are not hurt, because of the size of their treasuries, when it comes to complying with these sections, but the private flying industry is seriously affected.

I think it would be useful at this stage to consider the extent to which private flying in Canada has grown in the past few years. As of June 30 this year, official Department of Transport records showed that there were 6,381 Canadian civil aircraft on the registry. Of those only 5,242 had valid certificates of air worthiness. If we compare this situation with that existing in the United States, we find that in that country there were in excess of 8,000 private aircraft on the registry. Most other countries in the world have substantially lower numbers of private airplanes on their respective registries. The fact then emerges that Canada, amongst all the nations of the world, has the second largest private air industry in existence. This is quite a phenomenal growth from the days when transportation was by horse and buggy, by train or by automobile.
We are now faced with legislation that is designed specifically to curb Canada's private air industry. The fees which it is intended to levy against private airplanes using D.O.T. facilities, as the minister has stated, will greatly increase the revenues of the department. I feel, however, that the imposition of a one dollar landing fee at Toronto international airport, Montreal and Vancouver, whether on a private aircraft or any aircraft using these facilities, is not going substantially to increase the revenues of the department. I think, therefore, a valid argument could be made, and I would hope the minister would give serious consideration to it, for changing the section as it applies to private aircraft in respect of these landing fees.
The airports of this country are there for the benefit of all Canadians, just as are the highways. It seems to me wrong in principle that a landing fee should be charged the operator of a private aircraft who goes into a government airfield, just as it would be wrong for an automobile user to pay a toll on the trans-Canada highway. It seems to me that the aircraft owner is already a taxpayer. He contributes towards the cost of these Department of Transport facilities in the same way an automobile owner contributes through his taxes towards the construction of highways. Why should the private owner pay double taxation simply because he chooses one form of transportation over another?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CHARGES FOR USE OF FACILITIES AND SERVICES
speechtext: Does he pay tax on gasoline?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CHARGES FOR USE OF FACILITIES AND SERVICES
speechtext:
Yes, taxes are paid by aircraft users who purchase gasoline. There is a special tax on gasoline products purchased at most airports across the country. In Ontario, the tax is 17 cents, I think, although certain rebates are granted in most cases. Additional taxes to those paid by automobile

users are imposed on the users of aircraft fuel. This is a provincial source of revenue, I believe, and has no significance so far as the federal government is concerned. For the life of me, I cannot see how the private aircraft owner who is charged a dollar whenever he lands at Toronto, Vancouver or Montreal, is going to make any substantial contribution to the federal treasury. Think of the harm the imposition of this fee will cause. It already has caused harm in Montreal, and I believe the minister or his officials have received representations from organizations in this country who have brought this matter to his attention.
The business concessions at these airports which dispense fuel, the flying clubs which heretofore have been visited frequently by the private aircraft owner who had the privilege of using these services before, are no longer used to the same extent by him as they were before the imposition of these fees. While I am talking about fees, perhaps the minister might explain something to me. It seems to me that the purpose of the bill is the imposition of these fees against private aircraft using these D.O.T. facilities, and yet the fee is already being charged. This is a matter that perhaps requires explanation. If the fees have been charged without authority, then there seems to be something wrong.
There is another sector of the economy that is going to be affected by the imposition of these fees. As the minister knows, there are no national airports in the United States, the airports being owned by municipal or civil authorities. Consequently, there are no national laws requiring the payment of landing fees or other payments for the use of nationally provided facilities. In fact, there is complete freedom in the United States to use these facilities for air travel without any charge whatever. What we are doing is imposing on the United States air travellers who come to this country in great numbers, a nuisance tax-because that is in effect what it is. The air traveller has to land, walk into the airport manager's office and pay one dollar. As I have said, I think that this is going to discourage a great deal of tourist traffic, particularly in the Toronto, Vancouver and Montreal areas.
I want to say a word or two about one or two of the other regulations which I think impose an undue restriction on the growth of the private air industry in this country. One of them is the present air navigation order No. 7, series 1, which sets forth that the owner of a private aircraft is exempt from certain air regulations in respect of claiming compensation by way of rebates on income taxes and the like, if he uses his aircraft on his employer's business.
Aeronautics Act
He can, under the air regulations, be reimbursed for the use of that aircraft if he is travelling on business, but the anomaly in this regulation is that he is the only one who can claim such reimbursement and before he does so he must receive prior approval from the air transport board. Having regard to the speed with which any government agency operates, hon. members can see immediately that where a private aircraft owner is using his aircraft for a business trip he has to plan weeks and months ahead, in order to write to the air transport board to obtain approval before he can obtain reimbursement.
The provision is workable so far as large companies are concerned, with respect to large fuel costs; but nowadays many small businesses are using private aircraft, and if the owner of a small business uses an aircraft to transport his employees from one place of business to another place of business in Canada, the owner of the aircraft can claim reimbursement only for himself. If he takes his accountant, his solicitor, or any other of his staff on that private air journey and just for business purposes, he cannot claim reimbursement under the existing regulations. I think this is an unduly restrictive provision of the air regulations, and is one which is deserving of the minister's very serious consideration.
It would be just as strange to hon. members as if a person using his automobile on business in the province of Ontario had to write to the Department of Transport if he wished to claim allowances when he uses his own automobile for business purposes. Certainly under the provisions of our present legislation the owner of a private automobile, if he moves from A to B on business, can carry the employees of his business with him and obtain reimbursement for travelling expenses. Therefore I cannot see why the owner of a private airplane, which he is using in the course of the conduct of his business, cannot be entitled to claim the same reimbursement. The aircraft is becoming more and more an accepted means of transportation, and it should be viewed in that light.
The other matter which I would like to draw to the minister's attention covers the allowances now in existence under the legislation, permitting a privately owned aircraft to be depreciated. A person in business who owns an automobile and uses it for business purposes is allowed certain depreciation allowances, and those allowances, while they may not be generous, are regarded as being sufficiently broad so that the businessman has no doubt as to when he may claim depreciation and when he may not.
But the private aircraft owner is not so fortunate. Again these matters do not apply

Aeronautics Act
to the commercial operators, but they certainly do to the private operators. Right now the sleuths in the Department of National Revenue are down on the necks of practically every business that operates a private aircraft for business purposes. It is an uphill battle and struggle to claim reasonable depreciation allowance on privately owned aircraft that are used in the businesses of the owners.
I mention one organization about which I am sure the minister has heard. It is the Canadian owners and pilots association, with headquarters here in Ottawa. I am sure they must have made representations to the minister with respect to the imposition of the fees being called for by this legislation. They publish a magazine called "Canadian Flight," and in the April-May issue of this year, and again in the October-November issue, editorials set forth their objections to the imposition of these fees. I read from the April-May issue where the editorial has this to say:
The latest move in what is obviously a creeping campaign to discourage the use of major airports by small private aircraft is the imposition by the Department of Transport of landing fees for private aircraft at Vancouver, Toronto and Montreal. And to make the pill even harder to swallow, the department at the same time has announced rate increases of up to 50 per cent for outside storage of aircraft at various D.O.T. airports across the country.
This is another matter which is not covered by the regulations, and to which I take serious objection. The minister has airports under his jurisdiction all across the country, with hangars standing on them empty, or filled with farm equipment, or material other than aircraft. Over the past few years I paid rent for storage in a hangar at Whitehorse at a cost of $30 a month. This year, the rate has been increased to $50 a month, and this is not the type of policy that will induce Canadian citizens to engage in flying activity.
I think it is desirable to encourage the growth of a private air industry, but we are certainly not going to do it by following a policy that is going to utilize hangars, which should be made available for aircraft at more reasonable rates, for the storage of farm and other equipment. Also the rates for outside storage have been increased by 50 per cent. Even just to tie an aircraft down on a D.O.T. managed airport costs $18 a month, and the aircraft may suffer from snow-blowing equipment that scatters ice and rocks over it.
The editorial goes on to say:
Even if these decisions were justified-and that is a highly debatable point-the manner of their introduction has proved to be irritating in the extreme and has stirred up a violent storm of opposition in all parts of the country. In the first place, the new levies were imposed with virtually no warning at all, thus making it impossible for the affected parties either to present

opposing arguments or to plan a switch in their operations to other airports. Nor has D.O.T. offered any suitable alternatives to those aircraft owners who are being "pressured by price" away from the major airports.
Here we seem to have a very confused policy with respect to the decisions of the Minister of Transport. Anybody who has read the press or listened to the debates in this house over recent months, must realize that the Department of Transport is trying to separate the light aircraft training operations from scheduled aircraft movements. I only need to quote the exchanges which have taken place in this house with regard to the Penhold training base, and with regard to the Edmonton air base, as being prime examples of this confusion in policy.
I think I can do no better than quote the minister as recorded in Hansard for October 1 at page 2888 where he says in part:
Because of the capacity of the international airport, the size of which was increased during the construction period, I see no need to hold the city to its earlier commitment that it maintain a secondary airport.
He was referring to the city of Edmonton, and this is obviously opening the way towards federal concurrence in the discontinuance of services at the municipal airport. In other words, the minister is saying the new airport in Edmonton can absorb all the flying activity, which includes training schools and scheduled flights.

That is going to be the result of it because the small aircraft mainly used the municipal airport. The majority, perhaps 90 per cent of the private aircraft owned in the Edmonton area, use the municipal airport. If that airport is closed down-which seems to be the likelihood because it seems the minister is in favour of that idea, judging from what I read of his remarks, anyway; and perhaps he can clarify this matter-all those private aircraft will be forced to go to the Edmonton international airport. I believe we have a direct conflict here. If that is to be the policy, how does it stand when you set it side by side with closing the Penhold air base, simply because in the opinion of the minister and the government jet flying training in that vicinity interferes with the commercial operation. I do not agree with that either. This also has to do with facilities which are being closed down and which I think are very, very necessary to the safety of aircraft navigation in this country.
At the Portage la Prairie base, for instance, the jet training station was right in the middle of an airway. The radio range in the area was bent. I am sure the minister has been advised by his officials that it is possible

to bend radio ranges so that air traffic can be routed around dangerous areas. They do it in mountainous areas and other areas in which there are obstructions to safe navigation. It seems to me that very little difficulty would be encountered in bending the range at Red Deer, Calgary and Edmonton if it were felt desirable to have jet training operations at Penhold. The Portage la Prairie base, for instance, is right on the edge of the airway at the moment, the airway being ten miles wide. There is no technical difficulty that I can see in bending the radio range so that commercial air traffic can be routed as far as 20 miles away on a dog leg around the Penhold air base. If that is the only reason for not going ahead with the jet training program at Penhold, it is a very flimsy one. I think the minister's technical advisers will tell him that what I have been suggesting- that is, bending the radio range-is very, very possible.
The Department of Transport, as I understand it, has ordered all training away from terminal areas. I would like the minister to clarify this when he replies to these remarks. My understanding of the instructions which have been issued by his department is that it is going to be the policy to get training away from terminal areas and to use secondary airports, or encourage the building of more secondary airports, and encourage private and light aircraft to use those secondary or other airports. There exists, in my View, a very serious confusion in policy here, and I think it requires clarification.
I want to get back to rates, Mr. Chairman. I think the decision to raise the rates for outside storage is particularly hard to defend. The editor of "Canadian Flight", which is the official publication of the Canadian owners and pilots association says:
At many airports, private aircraft are allotted space on land that the D.O.T. does not use and on which no maintenance or servicing expenditures are made. In return for a 50 per cent increase in rates for use of this land, the aircraft owner is being offered no additional services or benefits of any consequence.
The new tariffs will impose a greater hardship in some areas than in others. Because of a variety of factors, Vancouver seems to have been dealt the severest blow-
I am sure that hon. members on both sides of the house who come from the Vancouver area will have these facts in mind when they come to support this legislation, if they intend to so support it. This article continues:
-with the result that a new province-wide organization of aircraft owners has sprung up, practi-cially overnight, in order to fight this legislation.
I am sure that the new organization has made representations to the minister. There was a meeting last November in Alberta of
Aeronautics Act
the C.O.P.A., the Alberta aviation council and the new B.C. organization. Out of that meeting came certain resolutions with respect to these new rates. The support this new B.C. organization received was such that within a ten-day period the organization was able to finance itself, set up 13 committees and send a delegation to Ottawa. Surely the minister considers this rather convincing evidence, if any were needed, of the unpopularity of the latest Department of Transport action against private aviation.
If we read the provisions of this bill we see that most of them are designed as an invasion of what I consider should be the prerogatives of private aviation in this country. Certainly the air transport board is a very necessary organization. There is no doubt whatsoever that the highest possible standards of flight safety have to be maintained in a country such as ours, which has experienced such a rapid growth in aviation technology and use in recent years. Tragedies are going to occur. I think many people misunderstand and miscalculate the comparisons that are made between travel by air, travel by road or by any other method of transportation. I think it is very interesting, in this connection, to look at the figures. Very recently the dominion bureau of statistics drew up a comparison of accident rates of motor vehicles and aircraft. Private aircraft in Canada do not have to report the miles travelled, so these comparisons can only apply to Canadian aircraft other than those privately registered or those owned by government departments such as the departments of forestry in Ontario and Saskatchewan. In the three years 1959, 1960 and 1961 the average number of fatalities per 1 million motor vehicle road miles was 5.9, according to the bureau of statistics. For the same three year period the fatalities which occurred as a result of aircraft accidents in Canada averaged .022 per 1 million air miles. So the motto perhaps might be "Be very careful when you drive to the airport". I think these statistics testify to the level of safety which has been achieved by the commercial air industry in this country.
The air transport board and other divisions and branches of the Department of Transport which have been concerned with flight safety in this country have contributed to this very enviable record of safety in air travel in Canada. But I do not think we should confuse the desirability of encouraging the growth of safety factors in the commercial air industry in Canada with the undesirable effect produced by government agencies suppressing the growth of the private air industry. For instance, I can take one clause of the bill, clause 2, which purports to clothe

Aeronautics Act
the government with the authority to stipulate the maximum hours of work and other working conditions for pilots, co-pilots, navigators and flight engineers employed by any person operating a commercial air service licensed by the air transport board. This is a very necessary thing as far as large commercial operators are concerned. They have to maintain high standards of health in pilots, co-pilots and air crews generally who are flying machines of the size and complexity of the DC-8. But I wonder how much consideration was given by the drafters of this legislation to the operator of the helicopter service who is operating, say, out of Inuvik, Dawson Creek or Prince George, or to the operator of a fixed-wing operation across the Arctic, because the regulations apply to those pilots, navigators and flight engineers as well. I do not think very much consideration was given to the small, private operator of a commercial air service in Canada, because with the seasons as short as they are in the north country, and with the exacting standards of work placed upon these operators by government departments such as the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys in their laudable desire to get work accomplished as quickly as they can, these operators are taxed to their limit.
The pilot of a helicopter carries an engineer with him wherever he is operating under contract with the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. That engineer is on duty 24 hours a day. If there is a regulation proposed in clause 2 of the bill imposing a restricted number of flying hours on commercial pilots, it not only applies to commercial pilots flying DC-8's, if no exceptions are made, but also to operators flying a Bell helicopter in the north country, or a Cessna 180, or a -Beaver, an Otter, or a Norseman in northern Ontario.
Another clause of the bill which seems to invade not only the rights of private operators of commercial air services but also involves the rights of individuals is clause 3, where a board of inquiry is going to be set up to investigate aircraft accidents. That is a very laudable feature of the bill, but nevertheless I wonder if the evidence given before such a board, as is usual in air transport board hearings or hearings involving government departments, will be made available to the general public. For instance, if I were to testify before such a board, what disposition would be made of the evidence that I give? This matter gives me some concern.
I should like to say that in my view the Canadian public has come to accept the aeroplane as a primary means of transportation. The versatility of use to which an aircraft can be put bears this out. For example, pleasure

flying, flying for business purposes, for agricultural purposes, such as crop spraying and the like, are only a few of the many forms of activity which comprise our aviation industry, other than that part which most people think of in terms of T.C.A. or C.P.A., and other large air lines. All of these flying activities have become essential to our modern way of life, and aircraft owners in Canada, as I have shown from the statistics I have put before the house, are on the increase. The industry should be encouraged to grow. I think the public requires that the benefits of transportation in all its forms, including aviation, should be widely available at low cost, and with the minimum imposition of tariffs and inconvenience. The imposition of fees such as those which are going to be authorized by this bill are not going to contribute at all to the growth of private aviation in Canada. In my view they are going to retard the free use of the private aeroplane.
There is one feature the hon. member for Three Rivers mentioned a moment ago with regard to over-flights and the endeavours of the government to impose certain fees on foreign carriers flying over Canada and using Canadian facilities. As I see it, the hon. member for Three Rivers suggested that the government had abandoned its attempt to impose these fees. I hope that is the case. However, my reading of the first clause of the bill indicates to me that the government may, if it wishes, impose these very fees. As the clause reads now, it will allow the governor in council to make regulations to impose any fee or charge for the use of any facility provided by or on behalf of the minister in respect of any aircraft. Those facilities include radio ranges and non-directional beacons, as well as airports; in fact, every single facility that is provided by the Department of Transport for air navigation in this country.
Here I want to mention the policy of the department of discontinuing the use of radio ranges. Hon. members know how airplanes get from point A to point B in this country in weather conditions which do not allow one always to look at the ground. The facilities used are radio navigation facilities. The basic facility, which has been with us now for 20 years, is the air radio range station. The policy of the government now is gradually to close down these radio range stations. This is being done in a phased fashion, but I think it is a wrong decision to make. First to go in the radio range station is voice communication. Next to go is the station itself. These stations are being replaced with what are known as non-directional beacons. That is all very good for the large air services. They can operate because they have thousands and

thousands of dollars worth of radar equipment in their aeroplanes and have advanced radio aids which are being installed by the department, and very properly so. But I would again turn the minister's attention to the private aircraft industry in this country, which involves some 5,000 aeroplanes actively flying around the country which have not got this type of facility. Even if they could get it the aircraft would be too small for its installation. These aircraft are left with a diminishing number of aids to navigation. As a matter of fact, the discontinuance of these services is taking place so rapidly in Canada that the "Canada Air Pilot" cannot even keep up with them. One can pass a radio range these days and attempt to report, and the "Canada Air Pilot" has made no mention of the fact that voice communication has been discontinued at that radio range. The first thing that pilot knows is that he is reported missing because he has not reported, after having planned to report at that particular station. I am thinking in this instance of Brandon, where voice communication has been discontinued. I should like to support any move which would result in a saving of funds to the Canadian taxpayer, but 1 do not do so if it be inconsistent with the safety of air navigation. I very seriously question whether the government policy of discontinuing operation of radio ranges in this country is sound, because I think it is going to impair the safety of air navigation, not of the large carriers but certainly of the smaller carriers.
On the other hand, on the credit side, some of the facilities offered by the Department of Transport to the air industry in Canada are very desirable indeed; for instance, the development of ultra high-frequency equipment and the authorization of a continuous wide area of broadcasting of aviation weather over the Toronto low-frequency radio range. This is of benefit to every pilot flying in southern Ontario. I understand that this is being done on an experimental basis, and I would urge the minister to do it in other areas of Canada as well.
These facilities, as with airports, are services provided by the Canadian taxpayer. One of these taxpayers is the private aircraft user, the private aircraft owner, and it seems to me that if he has to pay for these very desirable services he is, in effect, paying double taxation. I have already made the analogy of the use of an aeroplane and air highways and the use of an automobile and ground highways. There should be no taxation of the private aircraft user any more than there should be taxation of the automobile user in the form of direct fees for the 28902-5-347
Aeronautics Act
use of facilities. If airport charges are to be made-and certainly clause 1 of the bill gives this authority to the government-I see no reason why the clause could not also be extended to tax private aircraft users using radio ranges and other like facilities.

speechtext: I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but his time has expired.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CHARGES FOR USE OF FACILITIES AND SERVICES
speechtext:
I was
interested to notice the intention of the minister, as indicated on the order paper, to introduce amendments to the Aeronautics Act. If I am not mistaken, this is the first time since 1952 that the act has been before the house for amendment. I was hopeful that the hon. gentleman would have taken advantage of the opportunity afforded by these amendments to include something in this bill to revise that section of the act which makes provision for appeals to be made to the minister from decisions of the air transport board only by the air line which happens to be immediately affected or, perhaps I should say, by the one which has applied, and not by others which might be affected. However, having given consent last night to allowing the resolution stage of this measure to pass without debate, I suppose I cannot pursue this matter further at this time and that I will have to reserve any further comments I might have to make in this connection to a later date.
I regret I was called out of the house for a short time, with the result that I missed the opening remarks made by the minister in introducing this bill. He may have answered, then, some of the questions I have in mind and which I intend to raise in the course of these observations. If that should be the case, perhaps he would just indicate to me, when he replies, that this is the situation, in which case I will consult his earlier remarks when they appear in Hansard tomorrow.
As I see it, one of the principal amendments contained in this bill has to do with the power of the governor in council to make charges for the use of airport and other facilities provided by the department. One question which occurs to me is this: Just what additional charges are contemplated to the users of these facilities in addition to those currently charged? What impact are these extra charges, if any, likely to have on air line fares and passengers? I must say I cannot share the thinking of the hon. member who preceded me on this aspect of the subject. If I understood him correctly, he was inclined to think no charges should be levied upon private plane operators for the use of facilities provided out of public funds. It seems to me this is an area where it

Aeronautics Act
could very well be that those who use the facilities should pay for them to a reasonable extent. It is obvious that most Canadian taxpayers are not, now, and will not, at least in the foreseeable future be, in a position to fly around in their own planes. I really do not think an analogy can be drawn between the situation of a plane owner and of an automobile owner in our present society. As the owner and driver of an automobile I certainly feel I contribute substantially in the course of a year toward the operation of public facilities which enable me to drive around the country. I do not feel that an unduly high levy should be exacted from plane operators, but I feel there is some reason why they should be required to pay a reasonable amount to defray the cost of facilities provided out of public funds.
I was interested, too, in what the hon. member had to say about clause 2 of the bill which gives the governor in council authority to fix maximum hours of work and make other regulations governing the working conditions of pilots. As I understand it, this clause authorizes the making of regulations which are yet to be drafted. I fail to see how one can reasonably conclude that the hours of work and conditions of work of a pilot of a DC-8 would necessarily be those provided in the case of pilots of some of the smaller aircraft operated by the smaller commercial lines. I would like to say, however, as one who has occasion to travel not only on DC-8's but on some of these smaller aircraft, that as far as I am concerned it is the same hide which is involved whether I am travelling aboard a DC-8 or on a Norseman. I am just as concerned that the pilot of that small plane should not be endangering himself or his passengers because he is working under conditions of undue fatigue, or for other similar reasons, as I am that the captain of a DC-8 should be in good shape to do his job. The crash of a small plane might not be as spectacular as the tragic accident which took place recently, but its effects are just as unfortunate for those who happen to be passengers on the small plane. If the minister has not already done so I should like him to indicate what changes are contemplated in the present regulation with respect to the hours and working conditions of pilots, navigators and other flight personnel.
With these observations I think I will conclude, and await the reply to be given by the minister when he closes this debate. In the light of that reply I may have further questions to ask during the committee stage.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CHARGES FOR USE OF FACILITIES AND SERVICES
speechtext:
I did not mention aircraft parking fees, Mr. Chairman, as the minister thought I had. Since he has raised the subject, may I say that I do not believe aircraft parking can be compared to the parking of automobiles. This is, of course, one of the nuisances, the imposition of a fee for parking an aircraft on a D.O.T. airport. You cannot draw an analogy between an airplane and an automobile in this respect. They are just as different as night and day. In the first place, the main reason an airplane remains located on an airport is that it must have a large area of ground on which to land. Then, the aircraft, due to its design is not capable of being driven down city streets or highways. In effect, it is forced to remain at the airport. The aircraft owner has not any choice. The automobile owner has scores of

alternative places in which to leave his car, but his own property is the most common place.
The average Canadian taxpayer pays for many facilities which are constructed with the use of public funds. My general plea against the provisions of section 1 of this bill is that while an individual may never expect to use these facilities to which he has contributed, it is not merely those who use the facilities who benefit from them. In this case, the general public benefits from the facilities established at airports. The D.O.T. facilities are for public benefit and the individual is free to use them whenever he has the opportunity. I could refer to such facilities as parks, bridle paths in national parks, playgrounds, museums and so on, which are operated without fees. Airports are such facilities just as much as our highways are. They are part of the public transportation system, just as much as the highways and railways are. The users of airports should no more be subjected to excess tariffs than the users of highways or railways. I would add at this point that this argument applies only to those who use the facilities of D.O.T. airports in a private capacity and not to those operating in a commercial capacity.
Private aircraft owners of this country are just as much taxpayers as any other group of taxpayers. They have, as I said, already contributed to the cost of airports. If we start imposing fees on the users of airports in this country, and not just airports but all facilities, then we are going to have to expect the authorities in the United States and Alaska will impose the same kind of fees. This will only have one result and that will be to curtail private aircraft travel between the two countries. Taken in total it imposes a restriction on the use of some 14,000 to
15,000	private airplanes.
The minister has said it is not the intention of the government to impose the $64 per hour fee on foreign users of air facilities for overflights in Canada. I hope I am correct in that assumption because that is the basis upon which the following remarks are going to be made.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CHARGES FOR USE OF FACILITIES AND SERVICES
speechtext: In answer to a previous question on that point I said the matter had not yet been decided by the government, that it had not been up for decision.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CHARGES FOR USE OF FACILITIES AND SERVICES
speechtext:
Then, what the minister is asking the committee to do, because section 1 of the bill does not cover this aspect, is to grant authority so that it will be there in the event the government decides to use it. I think that, in itself, is a very dangerous thing to do. If the government does decide to impose a tariff on foreign air line users who use our

Canadian air facilities on overflights, then I suggest the foreign nation will impose a like tariff on Canadian aircraft using foreign facilities. I believe that was the position before the government changed. I think the minister is aware of this. If this government decides to impose this type of tariff, the United States will retaliate and so will Mexico and the other nations which have terminals used by Canadian air carriers.
I think what we should be doing is encouraging the free intercourse of commercial aviation in the world. Canada should take the lead and operate on such a basis. I do not think there is a move on the part of any other nation to impose such a fee as this tax on facilities which, in effect, are provided for safety in air navigation. This covers the use of the facilities so far as commercial air carriers are concerned. But consider for a moment the effect it would have on the users of some 8,000 private airplanes in the United States, many thousands of whom travel into this country and use our air navigation facilities. This clause would authorize the government to impose such a tariff on those users.
I have already stipulated my reasons for being generally opposed to the idea of placing a tax on facilities supplied by the department for air navigation in Canada. Here I do not speak of a tax for airport parking or a tax for landing at an airport, a tax incidentally which is already supplemented by the one cent per gallon gasoline tax, which is paid by everybody who buys a gallon of gas at an airport in Canada. But I am speaking also of the facilities in the way of radio ranges, weather services, and all the vast range of very desirable facilities provided by the department for the safety of the commercial and private air industry.
I do not think that these facilities should be taxed. The minister has left the implication with the committee that if these taxes are not imposed on the users of D.O.T. facilities, we will not be going ahead with the program for expanding our existing airports and navigation facilities. I do not think that is a valid argument. I think the government has a duty to provide these services for the benefit of all Canadians, and no particular segment of Canadians should be taxed for the purpose of paying for these facilities. The test is not who uses the facilities but who benefits from the establishment of them. My submission is that all Canadians benefit from the establishment and enlargement of these facilities, and therefore all Canadians should pay an equal amount for their construction and maintenance.
Aeronautics Act
Clause 1 in the bill establishes an order in council power which would allow very far-reaching regulations to be made, with no limits to the amount of tax that could be imposed with respect to the use of these facilities. If the government wished, it could make it so difficult, in terms of exacting tariffs on private aircraft users in Canada, that they would be forced to discontinue the use of our major airports and would be forced, if you like, to use farmers' fields. That is the effect of the provision as it now stands. I am not saying the government will abuse it to that extent, but the power is there.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CHARGES FOR USE OF FACILITIES AND SERVICES
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit me to ask him a question. I have been trying to follow his argument, which I take it, refers to paragraph (b) of the proposed new section 3A. As I read it, the last three words say "at any airport". I fail to follow his line of argument that that included such things as radio ranges and other aids to air navigation. As I understand it, paragraph (a) would apply to facilities for an aircraft on an airport, and paragraph (b) would apply to facilities other than for an aircraft on an airport. I wonder how he relates his argument to a charge on navigational aids.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CHARGES FOR USE OF FACILITIES AND SERVICES
speechtext:
If the hon. member would read the whole clause he would see the effect of subclause 2 is to give the minister the power-
-to impose upon the owners or operators, wherever resident, of any aircraft, charges for the availability during any flights of such aircraft within or outside Canada of any facility or service provided by or on behalf of the minister.
That covers every facility provided by the department, and includes radio ranges, beacons, I.L.S. systems, and every system used for navigation in Canada. I do not want to go through a list of them. There is such a wide variety of very excellent services, supplied by the department for the users of airways and air space in Canada, that it would be too lengthy to go through them all, but therein lies the very danger of giving to the minister these very wide powers for the imposition of this type of tax.
In principle it is wrong because the facilities are for the benefit of all Canadians. As such they should be paid for by all Canadians, and a particular segment of Canadians should not be taxed in addition to the taxes they already pay. Second, the minister has left the implication with the committee that the only reason the clause is being passed is to legalize something that has already been done, first of all with reference to the $64 per hour for overflights by foreign carriers, and second with respect to the fees now imposed, and

Aeronautics Act
which I have mentioned, at Vancouver, Montreal and Toronto. I ask for an explanation how these fees could be imposed-and I believe they have been in effect since April or May-when this legislation is not yet passed.
For all these reasons I feel that the clause is an extremely undesirable one and gives rise to all sorts of dangerous possibilities. It stifles the growth of the private air industry in Canada, and the minister himself has said that the government has not yet made up its mind as to whether or not the hourly rate will be charged for overflights. It seems to me the power is not necessary in that regard at the moment, and so far as taxing private aircraft owners in Canada for parking, landing, and using air navigation aids, I think it is not a very good principle to establish. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Winkler):
That clause 1 of Bill No. C-117 be struck out.
